title: Finish a wire splice: even the wire tips, then twist the connector on clockwise until snug
context: Electricians splice conductors in junction boxes every day (O*NET 47-2111.00, Electricians). The connector makers print it on every carton: strip the wires 16 mm (0.625 inch), hold them side by side with the tips even, and turn the twist-on connector clockwise until it is snug and no bare copper shows below its skirt. A wire whose tip sits short of the other is never gripped by the connector's coil, so it pulls out or arcs and heats the box; a connector that is only started is loose and leaves live copper exposed. Here someone has pushed the connector onto the tips by hand without turning it, and one wire has slipped back into the box, so only the other wire's tip is inside the connector.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. A galvanized steel junction box, 4-11/16 inches square (11.9 by 11.9 cm) and 5.4 cm deep, stands open face up, fixed to the bench, centered at x 30, y 0 (x 24.05 to 35.95, y -5.95 to 5.95). It has two screw tabs in opposite corners and a green ground screw on its back. Two black 12 AWG solid copper conductors with THHN insulation (3.3 mm across) come up through white plastic bushings in two knockouts in the box's back: the right wire at x 24.7, y -3 and the left wire at x 35.3, y 3. Each rises straight up to 9 cm above the table, runs along x to x 30 at that height, then along y toward the middle, and stands up again at y -0.17 (right wire) or y 0.17 (left wire), so the two stand side by side touching at x 30. Each is stripped 16 mm at its end. The left wire is fixed: its insulation ends at 12 cm and its bare tip at 13.6 cm. The right wire starts 12 mm lower (insulation to 10.8 cm, tip at 12.4 cm, its horizontal runs at 7.8 cm); it can be drawn up or pushed down along its own length through its knockout and stays where it is left (from 16 mm below the left tip to 10 mm above it). A red twist-on wire connector for two to four 12 AWG wires, 2.0 cm across its ribbed skirt, tapering to 1.2 cm at its rounded top, 2.8 cm long, with one white rib, sits loosely on the left wire's tip, its skirt at 12.8 cm, pushed on but not turned. Its coil is right-handed (it threads on clockwise seen from above), travels 4 mm per turn, first bites 2.5 turns above snug, and is snug with its skirt at 11.8 cm, covering the last 2 mm of insulation.
scoring: The scorer watches the whole run. The connector's angle is measured back from snug, where its skirt covers the last 2 mm of insulation; its coil first bites 900 degrees back, and it starts at 915. The right wire counts as captured if its tip was within 3 mm of the left one's (under one 4 mm turn of the coil) at the moment the connector came a full turn onto the wires, 540 degrees back, and it has not moved more than 2 mm since; backing the connector off past that point and putting it on again judges it afresh. The score is 0 if at the end the connector is less than a full turn on, if more than 90 degrees of its turning on, net or clockwise in total, was not done by a gripper holding it and rolling with it (fingers closed on its 2.0 cm width, tool point within 1.5 cm of its axis, pads on its length, so a swipe, a knock or an open hand around it does not count), if the right wire is not captured, or if a gripper still holds the connector or the right wire (fingers under 60 % open with the tool point within 2 cm of it). Otherwise: 0.25 if the connector is more than 180 degrees from snug, so bare copper shows below its skirt; 0.5 if it is 45 to 180 degrees from snug, covered but loose; 1.0 within 45 degrees of snug with both arms back home and still, or 0.9 if not. The arms count as home with each tool point within 3 cm of where it started, because they are put back so the workspace is clear for the next job. Success is a full score held for 1 s. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.9, 1.0. In a real trial, mark a line on the connector's top and count its turns from the video; afterwards check with a flashlight that no copper shows below the skirt, measure with a ruler that both wires' insulation ends within 3 mm of each other under the skirt, and tug each wire: a captured wire does not pull out.
reset_notes: Turn the connector counterclockwise until it comes loose, push the right wire back down until its tip is 12 mm below the left one's, and set the connector back on the left tip, pushed on by hand but not turned. Nothing is used up.
fidelity: All parts are true size, and the wires are stiff: the left is fixed and the right only slides along its length, staying where it is left. The coil is a thread model: the connector rides a slide and hinge driven to 4 mm per turn, held by a light torque, stopped 60 degrees past snug. The wires do not twist together or turn, so they need no holding; capture is scored from the wire's position when the coil grips. Off the coil the connector stays on the wires' axis, and the tug test is not scored.
